name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,154

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A bishop visiting an isle south of Harris and Lewis

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's place, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: taken as written
RR stands for Right Reverend, the style of a bishop
Coll is a small Hebridean island lying south of Harris

explanation.surface: A bishop on a pastoral trip to a small island in the Hebrides, below Harris and Lewis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harris and Lewis' reads as the Hebridean island Lewis and Harris, but Lewis stands alone as the definition. RR, for Right Reverend, is the usual crossword bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll, author of Alice in Wonderland, is the pen name; the first name alone points to his surname.

clue.text: Middle-of-the-road Atwood book?

blocks.note: first meaning: a reflective stud set in the centre line of a road
second meaning: a 1988 novel by Margaret Atwood

explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle-of-the-road' looks like a judgement on Atwood's book as unadventurous, but it literally describes where the road reflectors sit.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflective road studs are known by this name in Britain, and Margaret Atwood published a novel with the same title.

clue.text: A sprite, wood elf or goblin originally

indicators.note: these letters are what the name was made from at first, before being rearranged into its final form

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of small mischievous folklore creatures: sprites, elves and goblins.
explanation.walkthrough: The list of fairy creatures seems to be all definition, but the last three words are exactly the fifteen letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Goodfellow is another name for Puck, the mischievous fairy of English folklore and A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Play that’s short of a certain vocal performer

indicators.note: something vocal is voiced, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: 'a certain person' can be 'one'
a performer on stage, spelt here as it is pronounced

explanation.surface: A play that lacks a particular singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vocal performer' looks like a singer; it is a performer taken vocally. ONE plus ACTER gives ONE-ACTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-acter is a play consisting of a single act, so it is short compared with a full-length drama.

clue.text: A sentence in an old magazine

blocks.note: first meaning: imprisonment for the rest of one's days
second meaning: the American photo weekly that ceased regular publication in 1972

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a line of text printed in a magazine; 'sentence' is the legal kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A life sentence is the heaviest prison term, and Life was a famous American picture magazine of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Who wrote of Sam McGee’s funeral for example?

blocks.note: first meaning: the poet of The Cremation of Sam McGee
second meaning: a religious ceremony, of which a funeral is one kind

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like one question about who described a funeral; the poet's surname is itself a word for a funeral rite. Robert Service wrote ballads of the Yukon.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Service wrote The Cremation of Sam McGee, and a funeral is an example of a religious ceremony held for the dead.

clue.text: Pants with blue yarn, but no embroidery?

blocks.note: pants and shorts are both garments for the lower body
blue is the colour of the Conservatives, so a blue is a Tory

explanation.surface: Trousers sewn with plain blue thread, but left without decorative stitching.
explanation.walkthrough: Yarn and embroidery suggest needlework, but a yarn is a tale; to embroider a tale is to pad it out, and this one is kept brief. Blue means Conservative in British politics.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale told without padding stays brief, and a brief piece of prose fiction is the literary form named here.

clue.text: Port mother left out for Coe’s club mate

indicators.note: what is left out is omitted, so those letters are removed from the longer word

blocks.note: the great Dutch seaport
a dam is the mother of an animal

explanation.surface: A port city loses a mother, for a friend from Coe's club.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Coe's novel The Rotters' Club makes each member of the club one of these. Take DAM off ROTTERDAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow member of the club in Coe's novel title would be one of its rotters, a dated British word for a cad.

clue.text: More than one new pilgrim turned into an absconder

indicators.note: to be turned into something is to be transformed, so these letters are remade in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, part of the same pool of letters

explanation.surface: Several fresh pilgrims have become runaways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' does double duty: it completes the signal and also belongs to the letters. Mark Twain's travel book was subtitled The New Pilgrims' Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's book The Innocents Abroad carried the subtitle The New Pilgrims' Progress, so its title names a plural group of such pilgrims.

clue.text: Tried scattering seed around perhaps?

indicators.note: things scattered are thrown about at random, so these letters land in a new order
something placed around another surrounds it, wrapping its letters about the inner piece

blocks.note: taken as written
'say' and 'perhaps' both mark an example or a guess

explanation.surface: Someone attempted sowing seed broadcast, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' looks like a hedge on the whole surface, but it is a word for the inner piece; the scattered letters split in two to wrap it.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay is a formal verb meaning to attempt, so its past tense matches tried as a synonym.

clue.text: What’s inside pills passed around frequently outside a party

indicators.note: something passed around goes round another thing, so one piece encloses the rest
a word sitting outside another surrounds it, so the second piece goes within the first

blocks.note: tablets are pills
a direct synonym
CON is short for the Conservative party

explanation.surface: Describing a drug's ingredients, with pills circulating freely around a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's inside pills' reads as one phrase about drugs, but the definition stops after 'inside'. The containers nest: the party within the frequency word, all within the pills.
explanation.definitionFit: A table of contents lists what a book holds, so it tells a reader what is inside the volume before opening further.

clue.text: English university rings one abroad to check Germaine’s female

definitions.note: the answer is the noun that 'female' qualifies in Greer's title

indicators.note: to ring is to go round in a circle, and going round brings the word back to front

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
un is French for one
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: An English university telephones someone overseas to verify facts about Germaine's woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Germaine Greer's 1970 feminist book is The Female Eunuch; the clue gives the adjective and asks for the noun that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Greer's famous title pairs the adjective with this noun for a castrated man, so the missing word completes the title.

clue.text: Sentence say, without appeal, is able to be extended

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away from the word before

blocks.note: a stretch is slang for a prison term
taken as written
SA is short for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A prison sentence, perhaps, that has no appeal and can be lengthened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like it marks 'sentence' as an example, but it is a word of its own, losing SA to leave Y. 'Without appeal' sounds legal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stretchy is elastic, so it can be pulled out longer; the adjective describes material capable of lengthening.

clue.text: Olympic sport a long time after Thales, Chilon, et al

indicators.note: coming after means following, so the second piece is placed behind the first

blocks.note: rugby sevens has been an Olympic event since 2016
'for ages' means for a long time

explanation.surface: An Olympic sport arrived long after the ancient Greek philosophers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sevens is the seven-a-side form of rugby. Thales and Chilon are two of the wise men of ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Thales of Miletus and Chilon of Sparta were among the traditional group of wise men honoured in ancient Greek tradition.

clue.text: Unions kept secret suggestions about work

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: elements of something are hints or traces of it
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Trade unions keep quiet about ideas concerning their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unions' suggests trade unions, but these are marriages. Opus, abbreviated, is the crossword's usual musical or literary work.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who run off to marry without telling family have a wedding that is concealed, which is what eloping means.

clue.text: A knight’s mate in between idylls

indicators.note: the answer is contained in the words that follow, its letters straddling a word break

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A knight's companion appears between Tennyson's Idylls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In between' reads as one phrase, but 'between' supplies the letters. Tennyson's Idylls of the King include Geraint and Enid, which is the point of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid is the wife of Sir Geraint, a knight of the Round Table, in Arthurian legend and in Tennyson's poems.

clue.text: Gantry holding up a medicine graduate such as cured Lincoln?

definitions.note: elliptical for 'one such as cured Lincoln', naming the person

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it within, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: Elmer Gantry is Sinclair Lewis's preacher hero
MB is a Bachelor of Medicine
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lifting frame supports a young doctor, of the type that treated Abraham Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gantry' looks like a crane, but it is the surname of Sinclair Lewis's Elmer Gantry. 'Cured' is the meat-preserving sense: Lincoln's body was preserved for its long funeral journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln's corpse was preserved for the funeral train, and the person who preserves a body for burial practises that trade.

clue.text: Old poems recalled summer almost

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
to recall is to call back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: one who sums, an adder

explanation.surface: Someone remembers verses about a summer long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is the season on the surface, but here it is one who does sums. ADDE runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Poetic Edda is a medieval Icelandic collection of Norse mythological verse, so the name covers a body of ancient poems.

clue.text: Briefly go into decline over an African town …

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter is removed
turned over means flipped, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to go into a place is to enter it
to ebb is to decline, like a tide going out

explanation.surface: Briefly, a Ugandan town slides into decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go into decline' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'go into' and 'decline'. Entebbe in Uganda is famous for the 1976 hostage rescue, which the ellipsis to the next clue plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Entebbe is a town in Uganda on Lake Victoria, home to the country's main international airport.

clue.text: Mum stops drink reaching her boy: he had over 80 cases!

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so this piece fills a space inside the others

blocks.note: perry is an alcoholic drink made from pears
ma is an informal word for mother
a mother's boy is her son

explanation.surface: A mother prevents alcohol getting to her lad, who has an alarming number of crates.
explanation.walkthrough: The '80 cases' look like crates of drink, but they are legal cases. Perry is a pear cider, common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Erle Stanley Gardner wrote more than eighty novels about this fictional defence lawyer, each one a courtroom case.

clue.text: … famously old, spread out and left in a state!

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so the earlier pieces go within the last

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
to ted is to spread out hay to dry
standard abbreviation
NY is the abbreviation for New York state

explanation.surface: Continuing the African town: renowned of old, sprawling, and left in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread out' reads as sprawl, but ted is a farming verb for tossing hay. 'In a state' suggests a mess; here it is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known, so the adverb formed from it means in a well-known way, matching the adverb famously.

clue.text: Maybe Shelob’s one like the rest, but taller

blocks.note: first meaning: Shelob is the giant eight-legged monster in The Lord of the Rings
second meaning: in snooker, a cue rest with a raised head for reaching over balls

explanation.walkthrough: 'The rest' looks like 'the others', but in snooker and billiards a rest is a stick that supports the cue; this one stands higher.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's Shelob is a monstrous arachnid, and snooker players use a raised cue rest of the same name to bridge over balls.

clue.text: Title of Tremain’s sparsest novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so these letters take a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Naming Rose Tremain's thinnest novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book being named, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Tremain, the English novelist, published a 2010 novel with this one-word title about a disputed property in France.

clue.text: Saint hosts an old group, gathering for devil worship

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the home, so one piece holds the other within

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
Abba is the Swedish pop group of the 1970s

explanation.surface: A saint welcomes an old band to a meeting of devil-worshippers.
explanation.walkthrough: A saint playing host to a satanic rite is the joke; the old group is the 1970s Swedish pop band.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabbat is a midnight meeting of witches and demons in folklore, held to worship the devil.

clue.text: He scored runs in a cricket side

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
the off side is one half of a cricket field, facing the batsman

explanation.surface: A batsman made runs on one side of a cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored' looks like making runs in cricket, but it means wrote music: Carl Orff composed Carmina Burana. In cricket the off side is the half of the field the batsman faces when standing to play.
explanation.definitionFit: To score music is to compose or orchestrate it, and the German composer Carl Orff did exactly that.

clue.text: Sapper hero (kind of) clips drill to two short days

blocks.note: bulldog clips are a kind of strong spring clip for papers
to drum something in is to drill it in by repetition
MON abbreviates Monday and D abbreviates day

explanation.surface: A military engineer, a hero of sorts, cuts short a training drill to just two days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sapper' reads as an army engineer, but it is the pen name of H. C. McNeile, who wrote the thrillers about this hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Drummond, nicknamed Bulldog, is the gentleman adventurer created in 1920 by the author who wrote as Sapper.

clue.text: Who made up Harry Devlin’s last 2 of 8 charges?

blocks.note: the final two letters of the answer at 8 Down
wards are people in someone's charge

explanation.surface: Asking who invented a lawyer's final two of eight criminal counts.
explanation.walkthrough: Martin Edwards writes the Harry Devlin mysteries about a Liverpool solicitor. 'Charges' looks legal, fitting a lawyer, but means people under care.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Edwards is the crime novelist who created the fictional Liverpool solicitor Harry Devlin, so he invented him.

clue.text: Part-time chemist is miles off turning tungsten into diamonds

indicators.note: turning one thing into another converts it, so one letter is swapped for a different one

blocks.note: something miles off is a long way distant
W is the chemical symbol for tungsten
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: An amateur chemist is nowhere near converting a metal into gems.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Faraday was both chemist and physicist, so only part of his time went on chemistry. The tungsten-into-diamonds alchemy is the surface's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Faraday did important chemistry, discovering benzene, but is better known for electromagnetism, so chemistry filled only part of his career.
